title: Checkpoint: The A1 Boundary Examination
summary: A cumulative examination of sections eighteen to twenty, and the boundary exam of the level: the impersonal constructions, the demonstratives and determiners, and the prepositions taken as a whole system.

drills.stem: Complete: **Man ____.** (I find it difficult.)
drills.explanation: Adjectives in **-us** make their non-gendered form in **-u**: *sunku*. There is no subject for an agreeing form to agree with, and *sunkiai* would be the adverb.

drills.stem: How is *It is snowing* said?
drills.explanation: *sninga* has no subject and never will have one. English needs a dummy *it*; Lithuanian supplies nothing, and that absence is the construction.

drills.stem: **Filmas įdomus** and **Man įdomu** — what is the difference?
options: None; the two are stylistic variants.
The first says the film is interesting; the second says the speaker finds it so.
The first is past and the second present.
drills.explanation: A nominative with an agreeing adjective states a property; a dative with the non-gendered form reports a person's experience of it. English uses one word for both.

drills.stem: Complete: **Jai skauda ____.** (Her leg hurts.)
drills.explanation: *skaudėti* is impersonal: the sufferer stands in the dative, the part that hurts in the **accusative**. English makes the leg the subject and Lithuanian makes it the object of a subjectless verb.

drills.stem: Which of these are **correct**?
drills.explanation: *galima* is impersonal and can have no nominative subject: *aš galima* is impossible. The impersonals change only for tense — *reikia, reikėjo, reikės* — and never for person.

drills.stem: Why is *mano galva skauda* wrong?
options: Because the construction is impersonal: no possessive and no nominative, but a dative and an accusative.
Because the verb must be negated.
drills.explanation: *Man skauda galvą.* The possessive and the nominative both belong to the English sentence, and carrying them across is the commonest error a learner makes at the doctor's.

drills.stem: **Vakar lijo, buvo šalta ir man reikėjo dirbti.** How many nominatives does the sentence contain?
drills.explanation: None. All three clauses are impersonal, and *man* is a dative. English would need three separate dummy subjects to say the same thing.

drills.stem: What is the locative singular masculine of **tas**?
drills.explanation: *tame* — *tame name*, in that house. *tam* is the dative, *tuo* the instrumental, *to* the genitive.

drills.stem: Complete: **____ aukšte gyveni?** (Which floor do you live on?)
drills.explanation: **Kuris** asks which one out of a known set — the floors of the building. *Koks* would ask what **kind** of floor it was.

drills.stem: Which of these are **correct**?
drills.explanation: The third leaves the verb unnegated. A negative word requires *ne-* on the verb beside it: *niekur nevažiuoju*. Lithuanian doubles its negatives where English forbids it.

drills.stem: **Visą dieną** and **kiekvieną dieną** — what is the difference?
options: *Visą dieną* is *all day long*; *kiekvieną dieną* is *every day*.
*Visą dieną* is plural and *kiekvieną dieną* singular.
drills.explanation: *visas* in the singular is *the whole of*; *kiekvienas* is a distributive and distributes over separate occasions. Both stand in the accusative of time.

drills.stem: Complete: **____ oras man nepatinka.** (I do not like weather like this.)
drills.explanation: **Toks** is *such, of that kind*, and is the answer to *koks?* as *tas* is to *kuris?*. It agrees with *oras* in the masculine nominative.

drills.stem: Complete: **Mes gyvename ____ name.** (We live in the same house.)
drills.explanation: **Both** words of *tas pats* decline, each following the noun into its case; *name* is a locative, so *tame pačiame*. English has one invariable word here and Lithuanian two variable ones.

drills.stem: Complete: **Neskaityk ____ knygos.** (Don't read this book.)
drills.explanation: Two rules act at once: the negated verb takes its object in the genitive, and the demonstrative agrees with the noun wherever the noun goes — *šios knygos*.

drills.stem: Complete: **Vakar buvau ____ gydytoją.** (Yesterday I was at the doctor's.)
drills.explanation: **Pas** with the accusative is used of people, and covers both going to somebody's place and being there. *į* is for places only.

drills.stem: Complete: **Kiek mokėjai ____ bilietą?** (How much did you pay for the ticket?)
drills.explanation: **Už** with the accusative is *for* in the sense of payment. With the genitive the same word means *behind*, and with the accusative it also serves for *than*.

drills.stem: **Prieš namą yra sodas.** What does *prieš* mean here?
drills.explanation: *Prieš* is *ago* of time and *in front of* of place, and takes the accusative in both senses. *Behind* would be *už* with the genitive.

drills.stem: Complete: **Stalas yra ____ kambario.** (The table is in the middle of the room.)
drills.explanation: **Vidury** governs the genitive — it is a locative noun doing a preposition's work, which is why a genitive follows it.

drills.stem: **Po** governs three cases. Which pairings are right?
drills.explanation: No preposition in Lithuanian governs the dative at all. *Po* in its three senses is the strongest argument for learning every preposition together with its case.

drills.stem: How many cases are governed by prepositions at this level?
drills.explanation: Three: the genitive, which takes much the largest share; the accusative, chiefly of motion, time and payment; and the instrumental, which has only *su* and *po*. Nothing governs the dative, the nominative or the vocative.

drills.stem: **Mokausi lietuvių kalbos, bet dar nesimokau rašyti.** What has happened to the reflexive affix?
options: It has been dropped after the negative.
It has moved from the end of the word to just after *ne-*.
It has become a separate word.
It has changed into a prefix meaning *not*.
drills.explanation: Under negation the *-si-* migrates to the front: *mokausi* but *nesimokau*. Without this a negated reflexive is very hard to recognise, which is why it is worth knowing before the full paradigm.

drills.title: Toks oras
drills.passage:
Šiandien šalta ir lyja. Toks oras man nepatinka, bet nieko nepadarysi. Vaikščiojau po miestą visą rytą, ir dabar man skauda kojas.
– Kuriame name gyveni? — paklausė draugas.
– Tame pačiame, kaip ir pernai, virš kavinės. Ateik pas mane, jeigu nori. Bet lifto nėra, o aš gyvenu penktame aukšte.
– Ar tau sunku lipti?
– Kiekvieną dieną sunku. Bet jaučiuosi geriau negu žiemą: tada niekada neišeidavau.
drills.translation: Today it is cold and raining. I don't like weather like this, but there is nothing to be done. I walked about the town all morning, and now my legs ache. — "Which house do you live in?" a friend asked. — "The same one as last year, above the café. Come to my place if you like. But there's no lift, and I live on the fifth floor." — "Is it hard for you to climb?" — "Every day it's hard. But I feel better than in the winter: then I never used to go out."

glossary.nieko nepadarysi: there is nothing to be done
glossary.neišeidavau: I never used to go out

questions.explanation: *Šiandien šalta ir lyja* — a non-gendered adjective and a subjectless verb, the two ways of reporting the weather, joined by *ir*.

questions.stem: Which of these words in the passage point at or quantify something?
questions.explanation: All four. *Toks* is *of that kind*, *kuriame* asks which of several, *tame pačiame* is *the same*, and *kiekvieną* distributes over days. Each agrees with its noun in gender, number and case, as an adjective does.

questions.stem: How many prepositions does the passage contain?
questions.explanation: Three: *po miestą* (accusative, *about*), *virš kavinės* (genitive, *above*), and *pas mane* (accusative, to a person). *negu* is a conjunction and *tada* an adverb, neither of which governs a case.
